## Clinical background

[Cryptococcosis in kidney transplant recipients](https://academic.oup.com/ofid/article/12/5/ofaf263/8121609) is uncommon but potentially catastrophic. When [transmission occurs through the donor](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8096655/), it often presents early after transplant, may involve the central nervous system, and is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality despite treatment.

The costs of cryptococcus after solid organ transplant are unclear.  Although studies have quantified the cost of a single hospitalization for cryptococcus,
no study to date has estimated the total excess cost of care due to cryptococcus.

## What this analysis does

This project uses the [**United States Renal Data System**](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/about-niddk/strategic-plans-reports/usrds) to analyze the impact of cryptococcus on costs.



## Study timeline and cost trajectories {#study-timeline}

@fig-cost-timeline illustrates how the planned study windows relate to case and control costs. The 365-day eligibility lookback is longer than the monthly cost-outcome window. Disease-related care and diagnostic workup can raise costs before the recorded diagnosis, so the prediagnosis trajectory is part of what the study aims to describe.

![Conceptual study timeframes and mean cost trajectories; no patient data or study estimates are shown. The monthly outcome panel spans days −90 to 359. Earlier dashed curves provide context outside that panel. Shaded differences are illustrative and do not establish causal attribution.](quarto/assets/integrated-cost-timeline.svg){#fig-cost-timeline width=100% fig-alt="Line diagram of mean costs over time for cases and controls. The eligibility bar spans days minus 365 to minus 1. Pale dashed curves precede the cost-outcome window. During intervals minus 3 to minus 1, cases rise above zigzagging controls, peak near the case diagnosis or matched control index date, and decline gradually while remaining higher through interval 11."}

[Open the figure at full size](quarto/assets/integrated-cost-timeline.svg).

For cases, time zero is the first qualifying diagnosis claim; controls are aligned at the same time since their most recent transplant, so their calendar dates may differ. The figure explains the intended windows, not the completeness of observation: coverage loss, death, and partial months require the handling specified in the [analysis plan](quarto/analysis-plan.qmd). Earlier costs may also inform planned matching covariates; they are outside the monthly outcome panel shown here.

## Methods

We selected cryptococcus cases based on the following inclusion criteria:

- Age 18 or greater
- Prior kidney transplant
- ICD9 or ICD10 codes for cryptococcus (2 outpatient or 1 inpatient)
- One year of Medicare primary coverage lead-in

Controls were matched 2:1 to cases based on risk-set sampling on the following:

- Time since transplant
- Diabetes
- HIV/AIDS
- Age within 10 years
- Sampling date for control within 3 years of sampling date for case

Institutional claims data were abstracted as well as Physician/Supplier line-item data.

### Reproducibility

All analyses presented on this website are fully reproducible.  

The complete source code used to perform the full analysis and generate the tables and figures is publicly available at this [GitHub repo](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Cryptococcus-cost-analysis).  The R script `R/main.R` will run the R subscripts needed for this analysis in the order they are to be run.  Model assumptions, parameter values, and analytic workflows are documented in the repository to facilitate transparency and reuse.
